question.text: An Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) differs from a regular open-ended mutual fund in that an ETF:

answer.text: Is traded on stock exchanges throughout the trading day at market price
Guarantees a fixed return to investors
Does not have an NAV calculated daily

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook describes ETFs as funds that replicate an index, are listed and traded on stock exchanges, settle like stock trades through a demat account, and have prices that change in real time during market hours. Open-ended mutual funds, by contrast, are bought and redeemed at the end-of-day NAV computed at the close of business. That ability to trade on the exchange at a market price throughout the day is the defining ETF feature. The Trap: ETFs do invest across asset classes including equity, so Option A is wrong. No mutual-fund product, ETF or otherwise, offers a guaranteed return, ruling out Option C. ETFs still have an NAV, so Option D is wrong; the distinction is that ETFs also trade at a market price during the day while mutual funds transact only at end-of-day NAV. Note: The exchange-trading, real-time pricing, and demat-settlement features of ETFs versus end-of-day NAV transactions for open-ended funds are all drawn directly from the workbook.
